Is that safe?","fact_ids":["sec07-F03"]},"answer":{"text":"No. The car can get forty to fifty degrees hotter than outside, even with a window cracked.","fact_ids":["sec07-F03"]},"rationale":{"text":"Heat builds quickly inside a parked car, and children or animals left inside can suffer heat stroke or death.","fact_ids":["sec07-F03"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec07-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Hidden dangers around the car","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Pickup beds have exemptions.","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]},{"text":"Parked cars can harm passengers.","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"This chapter is about sharing the road safely with the people most at risk around vehicles: pedestrians, children, school bus riders, emergency workers and officers at traffic stops. It begins with two short topics about passengers. First, we finish the pickup bed rule for children from the last chapter, with its exemptions and its penalty. Then we look at two dangers that can strike even when the car is parked: extreme heat inside a closed car on a sunny day, and carbon monoxide that can build up when snow blocks the exhaust pipe in winter.","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Pickup bed exemptions","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"A supervising adult in the bed.","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02"]},{"text":"An emergency or a parade.","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02"]},{"text":"Farm work.","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"The rule against children under sixteen riding in an open pickup bed has exemptions. It does not apply when a supervising adult rides in the bed, in an emergency, in a parade, or while the vehicle serves an agricultural enterprise, such as work on a farm. Breaking the rule brings a ticket and a twenty-five dollar fine. It is an infraction with no court costs, no license points and no insurance surcharge. So the penalty is small, but the risk is not. An open bed offers no seat belts, no walls and no protection if the truck brakes hard or crashes.","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Heat and carbon monoxide","fact_ids":["sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Sun can heat a car forty to fifty degrees.","fact_ids":["sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]},{"text":"Cracked windows do not help enough.","fact_ids":["sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]},{"text":"Snow-blocked exhaust brings carbon monoxide.","fact_ids":["sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"A parked car in the sun can get roughly forty to fifty degrees hotter inside than outside, even with a window cracked, so leaving children or animals inside can cause heat stroke or death. Winter has its own danger. If snow blocks the exhaust pipe while the car warms up, carbon monoxide can be forced inside the car. This gas cannot be seen, smelled or tasted, but it is poisonous. So before warming up a car after a snowfall, clear the snow from around the exhaust pipe, and never leave anyone inside a running car with a blocked exhaust.","fact_ids":["sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u01-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"A cracked window is not enough","fact_ids":["sec07-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Heat builds even with a window cracked.","fact_ids":["sec07-F03"]},{"text":"A quick errand is still dangerous.","fact_ids":["sec07-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Many people believe a cracked window keeps a parked car safe for a few minutes. The handbook says otherwise: a parked car in the sun can get roughly forty to fifty degrees hotter inside than outside, even with a window cracked. Children and pets heat up much faster than adults, and a quick errand can stretch longer than planned. On practice questions, any option suggesting a cracked window or a short stop makes it acceptable is wrong. The safe rule is simple and absolute. Never leave children or animals alone in a parked car.","fact_ids":["sec07-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u01-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the parked car","fact_ids":["sec07-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Summer afternoon errand.","fact_ids":["sec07-F03"]},{"text":"Toddler left inside, window cracked.","fact_ids":["sec07-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: on a hot summer afternoon, a parent wants to leave a sleeping toddler in the parked car with a window cracked while running into a store for a quick errand. A parked car in the sun can get roughly forty to fifty degrees hotter inside than outside, even with a window cracked, and leaving a child inside can cause heat stroke or death. The parent should bring the toddler along. A few minutes of inconvenience is nothing compared with that risk.","fact_ids":["sec07-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u01-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Passenger dangers recap","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02","sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Pickup bed exemptions and a small fine.","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02","sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]},{"text":"Parked cars heat fast.","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02","sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]},{"text":"Clear snow from the exhaust.","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02","sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us recap. Next, pedestrians.","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02","sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec07-u02","module_id":"sec07-m02","objective_ids":["sec07-u02"],"title":{"text":"Pedestrian right of way","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F06","sec07-F07"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Pedestrians have no protection in a crash, so the law gives them the right of way in crosswalks and on green.","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F07"]},{"text":"Even when a pedestrian is in the wrong, drivers must warn and yield, because avoiding harm comes first.","fact_ids":["sec07-F11","sec07-F12"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Taylor is waiting to turn right on a green light while a pedestrian starts across the crosswalk on the same green.","fact_ids":["sec07-F07"]},"reasoning":{"text":"A pedestrian crossing on green has the right of way over every vehicle, including one turning across the pedestrian's path.","fact_ids":["sec07-F07","sec07-R08"]},"result":{"text":"Taylor waits until the pedestrian is clear before turning.","fact_ids":["sec07-F07"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a turning driver with a green light goes before a pedestrian crossing on the same green.","fact_ids":["sec07-R08"]},"correction":{"text":"A pedestrian on green has the right of way even over a turning car, though pedestrians should not start crossing on red or yellow.","fact_ids":["sec07-R08","sec07-F07","sec07-F06"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Green walker beats turning car.","fact_ids":["sec07-F07"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Taylor has a green light and wants to turn right, but a pedestrian is crossing on the same green. Who goes first?","fact_ids":["sec07-F07","sec07-R08"]},"answer":{"text":"The pedestrian.","fact_ids":["sec07-F07"]},"rationale":{"text":"A pedestrian crossing on green has the right of way over every vehicle, including turning cars.","fact_ids":["sec07-F07","sec07-R08"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Sharing space with walkers","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F07","sec07-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Crosswalks and signals.","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F07","sec07-F12"]},{"text":"Warn and yield when needed.","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F07","sec07-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"Pedestrians are the most exposed people on the road. They have no seat belts, no air bags and no metal around them. This lesson covers when pedestrians have the right of way at intersections with and without signals, what happens when a light changes mid-crossing, the special consideration given to blind pedestrians, how Walk and Don't Walk signals work, and the driver's duty to warn with the horn and yield, even when a pedestrian is in the wrong. These rules come up often on practice questions, usually in the form of a turning driver and a crossing pedestrian.","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F07","sec07-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Crosswalks without signals","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Marked crosswalks count.","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F09"]},{"text":"Unmarked crosswalks count too.","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F09"]},{"text":"Blind pedestrians get special consideration.","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"At an intersection with no traffic signals, pedestrians in a marked crosswalk have the right of way. So do pedestrians in an unmarked crosswalk, which is the space formed by extending the sidewalk lines across the street. In other words, a crosswalk exists at most intersections even if no paint marks it. At an unsignaled intersection, the law also gives special consideration to a blind pedestrian who holds out a white cane, a red-tipped white cane, or has a guide dog. If you see a white cane or a guide dog near the curb, stop and give that person all the time they need.","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Pedestrians and signals","fact_ids":["sec07-F06","sec07-F07","sec07-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Pedestrians follow the signals for their direction.","fact_ids":["sec07-F06","sec07-F07","sec07-F08"]},{"text":"Do not start on red or yellow.","fact_ids":["sec07-F06","sec07-F07","sec07-F08"]},{"text":"Green gives them the right of way.","fact_ids":["sec07-F06","sec07-F07","sec07-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Where ordinary traffic signals control an intersection, pedestrians follow the same signals as drivers going their direction, and they should not begin crossing on red or yellow. When a pedestrian crosses on a green signal, that pedestrian has the right of way over every vehicle, including one turning across the pedestrian's path. And if the light turns yellow or red while a pedestrian is still in the street, drivers must let that person finish crossing safely. So a change of light never gives a driver permission to push through a pedestrian who is already in the crosswalk.","fact_ids":["sec07-F06","sec07-F07","sec07-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Green walker, turning car","fact_ids":["sec07-R08","sec07-F07","sec07-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Pedestrian on green beats a turning car.","fact_ids":["sec07-R08","sec07-F07","sec07-F06"]},{"text":"Pedestrians should not start on red or yellow.","fact_ids":["sec07-R08","sec07-F07","sec07-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. A driver turning on a green light often feels entitled to go, because the light is green for them too. But a pedestrian crossing on green has the right of way even over a turning car. The turning driver must wait. On the other side, a pedestrian should not start crossing on red or yellow. Practice questions test both halves. When the pedestrian is on green, the driver yields, even while turning. When the pedestrian starts on red, the pedestrian is in the wrong, though the driver must still warn and avoid hitting them. Memory line: green walker beats turning car.","fact_ids":["sec07-R08","sec07-F07","sec07-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Walk and Don't Walk signals","fact_ids":["sec07-F10","sec07-R09"]},"lines":[{"text":"When operating, they override the lights.","fact_ids":["sec07-F10","sec07-R09"]},{"text":"Walk equals a green light for walkers.","fact_ids":["sec07-F10","sec07-R09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Some intersections have separate pedestrian signals. Where Walk and Don't Walk signals operate, pedestrians obey them instead of the regular traffic lights, and crossing on Walk gives them the same right of way as a green light. So when both signals are present and working, the pedestrian signal is the one that governs the pedestrian. A driver should therefore watch for people crossing on a Walk signal and treat them exactly as pedestrians crossing on green, including when the driver is turning. Walk and Don't Walk signals, when operating, override the regular traffic lights for pedestrians.","fact_ids":["sec07-F10","sec07-R09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s6","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Horn and yield duties","fact_ids":["sec07-F11","sec07-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Pedestrian steps out against red? Warn, stop if needed.","fact_ids":["sec07-F11","sec07-F12"]},{"text":"Yield even when they are wrong.","fact_ids":["sec07-F11","sec07-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"Drivers have duties even when a pedestrian breaks the rules. If you are going through on green and a pedestrian steps into your path against a red signal, warn them with your horn. More broadly, the law requires a horn warning whenever a turn, a stop, or a start from a parked spot may affect a pedestrian, and if the pedestrian keeps going, the driver must stop. You must yield even when the pedestrian is not entitled to it. The reason is simple. A right of way never justifies hitting someone, and the driver controls the far more dangerous machine.","fact_ids":["sec07-F11","sec07-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the right turn","fact_ids":["sec07-F07","sec07-R08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Green light, turning right.","fact_ids":["sec07-F07","sec07-R08"]},{"text":"Pedestrian crossing on the same green.","fact_ids":["sec07-F07","sec07-R08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: Taylor is stopped at a red light, which turns green. The answer is the pedestrian. A pedestrian crossing on green has the right of way over every vehicle, including one turning across the pedestrian's path. Taylor waits until the pedestrian has fully cleared the crosswalk, then makes the turn. The green light gave Taylor permission to turn, not priority over the walker.","fact_ids":["sec07-F07","sec07-R08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Pedestrian recap","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F06","sec07-F07","sec07-R08","sec07-F08","sec07-F09","sec07-F10","sec07-R09","sec07-F11","sec07-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Crosswalks, marked or unmarked.","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F06","sec07-F07","sec07-R08","sec07-F08","sec07-F09","sec07-F10","sec07-R09","sec07-F11","sec07-F12"]},{"text":"Green walker beats turning car.","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F06","sec07-F07","sec07-R08","sec07-F08","sec07-F09","sec07-F10","sec07-R09","sec07-F11","sec07-F12"]},{"text":"Warn, stop and yield.","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F06","sec07-F07","sec07-R08","sec07-F08","sec07-F09","sec07-F10","sec07-R09","sec07-F11","sec07-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, at intersections without signals, pedestrians in marked or unmarked crosswalks have the right of way, and blind pedestrians with a white cane or guide dog get special consideration. At signals, pedestrians follow the lights for their direction and should not start on red or yellow, but a pedestrian on green has the right of way even over a turning car, and anyone still crossing when the light changes must be allowed to finish. Must Jordan stop?","fact_ids":["sec07-F26","sec07-R01"]},"answer":{"text":"Yes. On a four-lane road with no median, both directions stop.","fact_ids":["sec07-F26"]},"rationale":{"text":"Only a median, a divided highway, or a wide road with a turning lane limits the stop to following traffic.","fact_ids":["sec07-R01","sec07-F24","sec07-F23"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec07-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Stopping for school buses","fact_ids":["sec07-F14","sec07-F16","sec07-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"When to stop and for how long.","fact_ids":["sec07-F14","sec07-F16","sec07-R01"]},{"text":"Which drivers must stop.","fact_ids":["sec07-F14","sec07-F16","sec07-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"School bus rules are among the most tested topics in any driver handbook, and among the most important. This lesson covers the school bus speed limit and the hours to be extra careful, when you must stop for a school bus and how long you must stay stopped, and then the part that confuses the most learners: which traffic must stop on each road layout. Two-lane roads, roads with a center turning lane, four-lane roads and divided highways all have their own answers. By the end you should be able to look at a road and know whether oncoming traffic stops.","fact_ids":["sec07-F14","sec07-F16","sec07-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Speed and school hours","fact_ids":["sec07-F14","sec07-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"School buses: no faster than forty-five.","fact_ids":["sec07-F14","sec07-F15"]},{"text":"Extra care seven to nine in the morning.","fact_ids":["sec07-F14","sec07-F15"]},{"text":"And two to four in the afternoon.","fact_ids":["sec07-F14","sec07-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"A school bus may travel no faster than forty-five miles per hour, so expect buses to move slower than the surrounding traffic on faster roads. Be especially careful during school bus hours, generally seven to nine in the morning and two to four in the afternoon. During those windows, buses stop often, children gather at bus stops, and young riders may dash across the road. A good habit during school bus hours is to slow down near bus stops and neighborhoods, cover the brake, and expect a bus to stop ahead, even if you cannot yet see its lights.","fact_ids":["sec07-F14","sec07-F15"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"When and how long to stop","fact_ids":["sec07-F16","sec07-F17"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop arm out or red lights flashing.","fact_ids":["sec07-F16","sec07-F17"]},{"text":"Stop and stay stopped.","fact_ids":["sec07-F16","sec07-F17"]},{"text":"Until arm in, lights off, bus moving.","fact_ids":["sec07-F16","sec07-F17"]}],"narration":{"text":"When a school bus shows its mechanical stop arm or flashing red lights to load or unload, approaching drivers must stop. And they must stay stopped until the arm is withdrawn, the lights go off and the bus begins moving. All three conditions matter. A bus with its arm still out is still loading or unloading, even if the children you can see have already reached the sidewalk. On a two-lane road, traffic in both directions must stop for a school bus that stops for passengers. So on an ordinary two-lane road, every driver in sight of the bus stops.","fact_ids":["sec07-F16","sec07-F17"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u03-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Not just until they cross","fact_ids":["sec07-R02","sec07-F16"]},"lines":[{"text":"Wait for the arm to fold in.","fact_ids":["sec07-R02","sec07-F16"]},{"text":"Wait for the lights to go off.","fact_ids":["sec07-R02","sec07-F16"]},{"text":"Wait for the bus to move.","fact_ids":["sec07-R02","sec07-F16"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Many drivers start moving as soon as the children they saw have crossed the street. That is too soon. The school bus stop applies whenever the stop arm is out or the red lights flash, and it lasts until the arm is withdrawn, the lights go off and the bus moves again, not just until the children have crossed. A child you did not see may still be coming around the bus, or one may run back for a dropped backpack. On practice questions, any answer that lets you go before all three conditions are met is wrong. Memory line: arm in, lights off, moving.","fact_ids":["sec07-R02","sec07-F16"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u03-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Both directions stop","fact_ids":["sec07-F25","sec07-F26","sec07-F17"]},"lines":[{"text":"Two lanes with a center turning lane.","fact_ids":["sec07-F25","sec07-F26","sec07-F17"]},{"text":"Four lanes with no median.","fact_ids":["sec07-F25","sec07-F26","sec07-F17"]}],"narration":{"text":"Two more layouts require both directions to stop. On a two-lane road with a center turning lane, all traffic in both directions stops for the school bus. The turning lane does not change the rule from an ordinary two-lane road. On a four-lane road with no median separation, all traffic in both directions also stops. Without a median, children crossing the road would have to pass through every lane, so every lane stops. A useful way to think about it is that if nothing physically separates the two directions of traffic and the road is not very wide, everyone stops.","fact_ids":["sec07-F25","sec07-F26","sec07-F17"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u03-s6","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Only following traffic stops","fact_ids":["sec07-F23","sec07-F24"]},"lines":[{"text":"Four or more lanes with a center turning lane.","fact_ids":["sec07-F23","sec07-F24"]},{"text":"Divided highway of four or more lanes with a median.","fact_ids":["sec07-F23","sec07-F24"]}],"narration":{"text":"On wider or divided roads, the rule changes. On a road of four or more lanes with a center turning lane, only the traffic behind a stopped school bus has to stop.
